I believe it will be nearly impossible to create a Moral Artificial Intelligence.

AI is ultimately a really complex series of algorithms. Or math equations if that is easier to visualize. The insurmountable problem seems to be math does not have a moral compass. Higher primates don't even have a moral compass. This is a uniquely human trait. So the questions become:

  1. What is a moral compass.
  2. How do we SIMULATE that in a computer.

There are broad definitions of what is and is not moral. Empirical evidence shows that any morality programmed by Silicone Valley would be seen by the overwhelming super-majority of the people in western civilization as little short of genocidal. So that is a nearly insurmountable problem right out of the gate.

But the real technical issue goes far deeper than that. The ONLY way to simulate morality in a computer would be for the programmer to put in hard coded conditions such that the AI would be prohibited from following its algorithms down a certain path - in practice many hundreds of thousands of paths. Even doing this would be far more difficult than a non programmer could ever understand. Within the bounds of "Artificial Intelligence" it is more than likely not possible at all.

A good example is the classic "3 rules of robotics". Such programming, if possible at all, would have to be placed as a final inhibitor, capable of throwing out the end results of countless hundreds of millions of computations. What is the program supposed to do next? It reached a "logical conclusion" based on all available data and made its best determination of an action. If it runs the analysis a million more times it will reach the same result a million more times, computers are very predictable that way.

But it gets worse. Say you can "push" the algorithms in a direction they find contradictory, to reach what they consider a "wrong" conclusion. What you end up with is not really Artificial Intelligence. One possible outcome of such end result short-circuiting that springs to mind is The HAL 9000 of "2001: A Space Odyssey". The best case scenario seems to be that in the end you find yourself with a really expensive, slower, and possibly, slightly more accurate series of "if-then-else statements" than we had in 1960.

Perhaps that is best possible outcome of all the AI hoopla. But before we try to build SkyNet we should revisit the best single piece of advice philosophy has ever given mankind: "Just because you can, doesn't mean you should".
